strengths: Addresses a genuine and important bottleneck: the edge-centric memory/compute cost of SO(3)-equivariant GNNs, and proposes a node-centric formulation with claimed O(|V|) activation memory.

Demonstrates real scalability: Table 3 shows E2Former-V2 running at 100k atoms where most baselines (EquiformerV2, MACE-Large, eSEN, E2Former-V1) OOM, with competitive throughput in both Conservative and Direct settings.

The memory-efficiency claim is empirically supported: Figure 4c/d show substantially lower peak memory than the naive PyTorch baseline, and the kernel design (online softmax, on-the-fly reduction, no edge materialization) is a reasonable hardware-aware contribution.
The overall direction—combining an SO(2) alignment/sparsification with the E2Former node-centric factorization and a fused streaming attention kernel—is a plausible and useful engineering synthesis.
An MD simulation (Fig. 5) is included as physical validation, and appendices document dataset and benchmark setup in some detail.
weaknesses: Central accuracy claim is contradicted by the paper's own table. Section 5.3 states the conservative variant achieves 'an aggregate Energy MAE of 1.27 meV/atom, matching eSEN-small,' but Table 2 lists E2V2-Cons. total E = 2.09 (1.27 is eSEN-sm-cons). This is a factual inconsistency that undermines confidence in the reported results.

Performance superiority is overstated. On SPICE, eSEN-Cons achieves 0.23 meV/atom vs E2V2's 0.53–0.57, so the claim of 'lowest Energy and Force MAE across most subsets' is not supported. On OMol25, E2V2 is roughly competitive with eSEN-small (and worse on energy for the conservative variant) rather than superior, so the 'superior performance' framing is not justified.

The headline speedups rest on weak baselines. The ~6x EAAS speedup (Fig. 3) is measured against e3nn's dense SO(3) tensor product rather than the directly comparable eSCN-style SO(2) implementation, so it largely reflects the well-known SO(2) reduction. The ~20x attention speedup (Fig. 4) is measured against a naive PyTorch implementation that explicitly materializes N×K×H×D tensors, not against an optimized sparse/FlashAttention baseline.

Disconnect between theory and implementation. The Wigner-6j recoupling is presented as a key contribution (Eq. 5, 'unify Wigner-6j recoupling with SO(2) sparsification'), but the actual pipeline (Eq. 8–10) uses plain tensor products with single R(r_j) and R(r_i) terms, not the sum-over-u 6j-recoupled form of Eq. 5. The relationship between the factorization theorem and the implemented computation is never explained, leaving the core algebraic claim unverified.

Presentation and notation problems. Lemma/Definition/Proposition numbering is inconsistent (Lemma 4.1, then 'Lemma 4.2 implies...', then Definition 4.2, Proposition 4.3). Definition 4.2 describes P as a 'blockwise linear map (acting independently on each degree ℓ)' yet the formula couples ℓ_i, ℓ_f, ℓ_o. Eq. 3 contains a typo (ψ_{m_2} for v_{m_2}); Section 5.1 has 'tow datasets'; the abstract ends mid-sentence ('The code is available at') with no URL.

Reproducibility concerns: the code URL is missing/truncated, and the Appendix B derivation of the EAAS re-indexing rule is informal (the complex-vs-real change-of-basis argument and the '-2(-1)^{m_o}' sign are asserted rather than rigorously derived).
The MD validation (Fig. 5) is qualitative only (an RDF overlay), with no quantitative error metrics or statistical comparison against MACE-OFF/experiment.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely bottleneck: the O(|E|) memory/activation cost of edge-centric equivariant GNNs, and proposes a coherent hardware-aware direction (algebraic SO(2) sparsification + fused streaming kernel).

The inference-scaling results (Table 3) are genuinely notable: E2Former-V2 is essentially the only Transformer-based model that runs at 100k atoms and is among the fastest in both Direct and Conservative settings (e.g., 1.24 steps/s vs GotenNet 0.27 in the Direct setting).
Reasonable engineering combination of known ingredients (SO(3)->SO(2) change of basis, FlashAttention-style online softmax streaming, Triton fusion) applied to the E2Former factorization.
Evaluation uses relevant, modern, large-scale benchmarks (SPICE, OMol25) and compares to recent baselines (eSEN, UMA, MACE, GotenNet, EquiformerV2).
weaknesses: Misreporting of the paper's own results. Section 5.3 states the conservative variant achieves an aggregate Energy MAE of 1.27 meV/atom 'matching eSEN-small', but Table 2 lists E2V2-Cons. total E = 2.09 (1.27 is eSEN-sm-cons). This is a factual error that misrepresents the method's accuracy and undermines the central performance claim.

Overstated accuracy claims. The abstract/intro claim 'superior performance' and 'lowest Energy and Force MAE across most subsets,' yet on SPICE ALL, eSEN-Cons (0.23 E / 6.36 F) substantially beats E2V2 (0.53-0.57 E / 7.8-8.3 F), and E2V2 is roughly on par with or worse than E2Former-V1 (force MAE 7.80 vs 7.46). No clear accuracy improvement is demonstrated.

Weak/confounded baselines. The '20x TFLOPS' and '~6x' speedups are measured against a naive PyTorch attention implementation and e3nn's dense SO(3) tensor product, not against optimized baselines (FlashAttention/SDPA, eSCN's SO(2) implementation, UMA kernels). Figure 1's 'Traditional EGNNs' curve is itself a PyTorch edge-centric attention baseline, so the comparison largely reflects kernel engineering vs. a naive baseline rather than an algorithmic advance.

Theory-implementation mismatch. The factorization theorem (Eq. 5) contains a sum over u with binomial coefficients and a Wigner-6j recoupling operator; the actual model (Eqs. 8-10) drops this sum. The claim that the implementation 'exactly' realizes the theorem and preserves exactness is therefore unsupported, and no equivariance-verification experiment is provided.

Limited originality. EAAS is essentially the eSCN SO(3)->SO(2) change-of-basis sparsification applied to E2Former's node-centric factorization. Despite the framing, the EAAS derivation (Appendix B) does not actually use Wigner-6j coefficients, so the 'unify Wigner-6j with SO(2) sparsification' claim is overstated.

Reproducibility gaps. The code URL is empty ('The code is available at' with no link). There are no training details (epochs, batch size, model size, compute budget, dataset splits), no hyperparameters, no error bars/variance, and the Triton kernel and the attention construction (Eq. 6, including the unexplained transpose) are insufficiently specified.

Insufficient ablation/analysis. No ablation separating the contributions of EAAS vs. the fused attention kernel, no accuracy-vs-speed tradeoff analysis, no direct comparison to eSCN, and only a single anecdotal MD RDF (Fig. 5) as physical validation.

Claim/evidence mismatch on training. The intro and abstract assert that large equivariant transformers 'can be trained efficiently,' but only inference throughput/memory is measured; no training-efficiency results are reported.

Presentation issues: numbering errors (the sparsity argument references 'Lemma 4.2' where Lemma 4.1 is intended), typos ('tow datasets', 'Tabl e'), and low-readability figures, which further hinder assessment.

strengths: Addresses an important scalability bottleneck in equivariant GNNs: the edge-centric memory wall and O(|E|) activation memory that limits large-scale atomistic modeling.

Proposes a plausible combination of node-centric factorization, SO(2) sparsification, and a custom fused Triton kernel for equivariant attention, which could in principle yield both algebraic and hardware-level speedups.
Reports strong empirical scaling on inference: throughput up to 100k atoms where many baselines OOM, and competitive accuracy on SPICE and OMol25 relative to MACE, eSEN, UMA, and E2Former-V1.
Provides useful appendices with benchmark protocols, dataset descriptions, and an attempted derivation of the EAAS re-indexing rule, which aids partial reproducibility of the experimental setup.
If the central technical claims were validated, the work could have practical impact for large-scale molecular simulation and foundation models.
weaknesses: Central theoretical claim of exactness is unsupported: Section 4.2 presents a three-stage flow h'_j = h_j ⊗ R(r_j), m_i = Σ α_ij h'_j, ĥ_i = m_i ⊗ R(r_i), which omits the binomial sum over u and the Wigner-6j recoupling in Eq. (5). As written, this is not equivalent to Σ_j α_ij h_j ⊗ R(r_j - r_i), so the method does not realize the stated E2Former factorization and the claim of preserving theoretical exactness is not justified.

The EAAS derivation is incomplete and potentially incorrect: Lemma 4.2 is missing or mistyped; the parity selection rule and sign factor −2(−1)^{m_o} in Definition 4.2/Appendix B are sketched rather than rigorously proved; notation m_i = m_o conflicts with the later statement that m_i is implicitly summed; and the re-indexing rule is not independently verified against e3nn or eSCN.

The invariant attention score in Eq. (6) is unclear and likely not rotationally invariant: concatenating W_Q1 h and (W_Q2 h)^T creates cross terms between different projections that may not transform correctly under SO(3), undermining the claimed invariant scoring.

The EAAS speedup is benchmarked only against e3nn’s dense SO(3) tensor product, not against existing SO(2)-based methods such as eSCN or eSEN that already reduce SO(3) convolutions to SO(2). Thus the claimed ~6× advantage over the state of the art is not established.

The fused on-the-fly attention kernel is compared only to a naive PyTorch edge-materializing implementation, not to optimized sparse attention kernels (e.g., FlashAttention with block-sparse masks, xFormers, or eSCN/eSEN kernels). The claimed 20× TFLOPS improvement is therefore relative to a weak baseline.

No training results are reported: despite claiming linear activation memory for training, the paper measures only inference throughput and memory; Algorithm 1 covers only the forward pass; backward pass, training activation memory, and training throughput are absent, leaving the main scalability claim for training unsupported.

Experimental claims are inconsistent with the tables: Table 2 shows E2V2-Cons total energy MAE 2.09 meV/atom, but the text says the conservative variant achieves 1.27, matching eSEN-small (1.27). Table 1 shows eSEN-Cons overall E 0.23/F 6.36, better than E2V2, contradicting the text’s claims of “lowest MAE across most subsets” and “superior performance.”

Reproducibility is insufficient: the abstract’s code link is blank; training hyperparameters, model sizes, L_max, channel widths, number of layers, data splits, random seeds, and compute details are missing; and the custom Triton kernel’s tiling, SRAM usage, recomputation strategy, and backward implementation are not described.

No explicit limitations section: the paper does not discuss failure modes, behavior at higher L, numerical stability from using absolute positions in spherical harmonics, or broader societal impacts. The MD RDF comparison in Figure 5 lacks quantitative error metrics or statistical significance.

Presentation quality is weak: there are numerous typos, missing references, equation errors, and unclear figure/table descriptions (e.g., Lemma 4.2, Eq. 6, Table 2 text mismatch), which impede verification of the technical claims.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely bottleneck: edge-centric materialization in equivariant GNNs, and proposes a node-centric formulation with the promise of linear activation memory and better scaling.

The EAAS idea of using SO(3)->SO(2) alignment to turn dense tensor contractions into sparse re-indexing is interesting, and Table 3 shows consistent speedups over e3nn, cuEquivariance, and OpenEquivariance on the tested tensor-product setting.

The fused Triton kernel eliminates explicit edge-level intermediates; Table 4 ablation shows a large end-to-end throughput gain (1.40 -> 4.24 samples/s at 5k atoms) and avoids OOM at 10k atoms, supporting the practical value of kernel fusion.
The empirical scaling results are promising: Table 5 reports scaling to 100k atoms on a single H20 GPU, with competitive accuracy on SPICE, OMol25, and OC20 S2EF-2M in the appendix.
The molecular dynamics validation, though limited, demonstrates practical applicability on liquid water RDF and a ~30k-atom solvated protein, which is useful evidence beyond static benchmarks.
The paper includes several appendices with derivations, training hyperparameters, benchmark setup, and additional experiments, which helps clarify some implementation choices.
weaknesses: The central claim of preserving 'theoretical exactness' is not adequately supported. Section 3 (Eq. 5) relies on Wigner-6j recoupling and a sum over u with binomial coefficients, but Section 4.2 implements a simplified three-stage flow using full R(r_j) and R(r_i) without the 6j recoupling, the sum over u, or the binomial factors. Appendix C only proves EAAS for a standard CG tensor product, not for the 6j recoupling used in the factorization theorem. The manuscript does not demonstrate that the implemented architecture is equivalent to the E2Former V1 factorization.

The EAAS re-indexing operator in Eq. (13) is poorly presented and internally inconsistent: it states m_i = m_o for both even and odd cases, while the odd case uses -m_i; the real-CG convention and sign factor -2(-1)^{m_o} are asserted rather than fully derived. The derivation in Appendix C is not rigorous enough to verify exactness.

Efficiency claims can be misleading. The abstract and main text claim 'up to 20x higher TFLOPS than standard implementations', but this is against a naive PyTorch sparse baseline, not optimized dense FlashAttention. Appendix J shows dense SDPA achieves much higher TFLOPS (e.g., 38.6 vs 1.95 at N=32768, D=64). Figure 1 also labels curves as 'Traditional EGNNs' and 'FlashAttention', but Appendix A reveals these are attention microbenchmarks, not full EGNN models.

Accuracy claims overstate the results. Table 1 shows eSEN-Cons has better aggregate Energy MAE (0.23 vs 0.31) and Force MAE (6.36 vs 7.05) than E2V2-Cons, yet the text says E2Former-V2 achieves the lowest MAE 'across most subsets' without noting the aggregate. Table 2 text says E2V2-Cons reaches 1.27 meV/atom matching eSEN-small, but the table reports 1.16 for E2V2-Cons and 1.27 for eSEN-sm-cons, an inconsistency.

Reproducibility is weakened by the missing code link: the manuscript says 'Our released code can be found at' but provides no URL. No Triton kernel code, EAAS implementation, or real-CG coefficient convention is released, making it difficult to reproduce the core claims.

The evaluation lacks statistical rigor. There are no error bars or repeated runs; several baselines are missing per-subset SPICE numbers; and the training schedule (Direct 17 epochs on OMol25 then 100 epochs on SPICE, Conservative initialized from Direct) may not be matched fairly for all baselines.

MD validation is mostly qualitative. The RDF and TM-score plots lack quantitative metrics or error bars, there is no baseline TM-score comparison for the protein system, 2 ns is short for protein stability claims, and simulation details (force field, timestep, thermostat, etc.) are not fully specified.

There is no limitations section. The paper does not discuss regimes where the approach is less beneficial (e.g., very small neighbor counts in Tables 6-7, where an edge-centric baseline can be faster) or where dense attention is faster in absolute throughput.

The end-to-end benefit of EAAS alone is modest: Table 4 shows 1.40 -> 1.55 samples/s at 5k atoms (about 11% improvement), while the main text advertises a ~1.5x speedup for the convolution stage. This discrepancy should be clarified.

strengths: Demonstrates a working node-centric equivariant attention system that scales to ~100k atoms with claimed O(N) activation memory, a practically meaningful engineering result (Tables 4, 5).

Predictive accuracy on SPICE and OMol25 is competitive with strong baselines (e.g., E2V2-Cons achieves 0.31 meV/atom on SPICE ALL and 1.16 on OMol25 total), so the efficiency gains are not obviously at the expense of accuracy.
Provides code release, detailed training hyperparameters (Appendix I), dataset descriptions (Appendix F), and component ablations (Table 4), which aid reproducibility.
Includes physically motivated MD validation (bulk-water O-O RDF and a ~30k-atom solvated protein) that goes beyond static benchmarks.
weaknesses: Overclaimed novelty. EAAS reduces SO(3) tensor products to a sparse axis-aligned SO(2) form, which is precisely the mechanism introduced by eSCN (Passaro & Zitnick, 2023) and used in EquiformerV2/eSEN, all of which the paper cites. The claim that these execution principles 'remain unexplored in existing SO(3)-equivariant architectures' is inaccurate; the pole-sparsity + sparse SO(2) re-indexing is standard.

The headline '20x higher TFLOPS' is measured only against a naive PyTorch edge-materializing implementation. Appendix J (Table 12) shows the fused kernel is actually far slower than dense SDPA FlashAttention (e.g., 0.609 vs 6.47 TFLOPS at N=32768, D=8; 1.95 vs 38.6 at D=64). The abstract's phrasing ('20x higher TFLOPS than standard implementations') is therefore misleading.

Text contradicts tables. Table 2 reports E2V2-Cons total energy MAE = 1.16 meV/atom, yet the text states 'the conservative variant achieves an aggregate Energy MAE of 1.27 meV/atom, matching eSEN-small' — 1.27 is eSEN's value, not theirs. Similarly, Table 1 shows eSEN-Cons better on ALL (0.23/6.36) than E2V2-Cons (0.31/7.05), contradicting the claim of 'lowest MAE across most subsets.'

The ablation undercuts the EAAS contribution: Table 4 shows EAAS alone improves throughput only 1.40 -> 1.55 (~1.1x), while the Triton kernel (a fairly direct adaptation of FlashAttention-style fusion to sparse attention) delivers the dominant gain (1.40 -> 3.31). The claimed ~1.5x EAAS speedup does not translate end-to-end.

Baseline mismatch in Table 3: the SO(2)-based EAAS is compared against SO(3) e3nn and against cuEquivariance/OpenEquivariance, rather than against the most relevant SO(2) implementations (eSCN/eSEN). This makes the efficiency claim structurally favorable by construction.

Weak baseline framing in Figure 1/Appendix A: 'Traditional EGNNs' and 'FlashAttention' are synthetic kernel-level microbenchmarks (QK + softmax + value aggregation on random inputs), not full architectures, yet the figure and text frame them as architecture-level comparisons. The masked dense-SDPA baseline is O(N^2) and is not a fair reference for sparse EGNNs.

Presentation problems: broken/garbled equations (Eq. 6 and the piecewise Eq. 13 are unreadable), incorrect reference years (Bartók et al. 2013 is listed as 'Batatia et al. 2013'; Batatia et al. 2022 is mislabeled), and duplicated references (Fu et al. 2025a and 2025b are identical). These hinder verification.

No limitations discussion. The Impact Statement is minimal, and the strong MD claims (TM-score monotonically increasing toward the native structure over 2 ns) are supported by a single system/seed with no error bars, no free-energy or stability controls, and no comparison to a baseline trajectory beyond MACE-OFF for water.

Training-efficiency claims in the abstract/intro ('training throughput and memory efficiency') are not clearly backed by training-throughput measurements; the main scaling table (Table 5) is inference-only, and it is unclear which results are training vs. inference.

strengths: Targets a genuine and well-motivated bottleneck: the edge-centric activation memory of equivariant GNNs. The node-centric reformulation plus fused kernel is a practically important direction for scaling equivariant transformers.

Strong scalability evidence: Table 5 shows E2Former-V2 scaling to 100k atoms in both Direct and Conservative modes while EquiformerV2, E2Former-V1, MACE-Large and others hit OOM beyond 10k–50k atoms, and it is the fastest at every scale reported.

Competitive accuracy: on OMol25 the Conservative variant achieves the best total energy MAE (1.16 vs 1.27 for eSEN-sm-cons and 3.62 for UMA-S) with force MAE close to the best, and on SPICE it achieves best per-subset energy MAE on Monomers, Dimers, Dipeptides, Solvated Amino Acids, Water and QMugs.

The evaluation is broad and layered: kernel-level benchmarks against e3nn/cuEquivariance/OpenEquivariance (Table 3), component ablation (Table 4), neighbor-density sensitivity (Appendix E), OC20 S2EF-2M results (Appendix G), and MD validation on bulk water RDF and a ~30k-atom solvated protein (Fig. 4).

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: training hyperparameters and backbone configuration (Tables 9–10), plus detailed benchmark/timing protocols in Appendices A and H, and an honest Appendix J that contextualizes the kernel's throughput relative to dense FlashAttention.

The Appendix J comparison with dense FlashAttention is a candid limitation discussion (acknowledging dense SDPA is faster in TFLOPS and explaining the FP32/irregular-gather reasons), which strengthens credibility rather than hiding the trade-off.
weaknesses: The headline efficiency claim is inflated by baseline choice. The abstract/introduction advertise 'up to 20x higher TFLOPS than standard implementations', but this is measured against a naive PyTorch sparse implementation, and Figure 1's 'FlashAttention' baseline is a masked SDPA that does O(N^2) work. Table 12 shows dense SDPA is far faster than the proposed kernel in raw TFLOPS (e.g., 38.6 vs 1.95 at N=32768, D=64). The speedup at large N is therefore largely asymptotic/against weak baselines and should be demonstrated against optimized sparse equivariant kernels end-to-end.

The EAAS derivation is not fully rigorous. Appendix C asserts a parity-dependent collapse (diagonal vs off-diagonal in the {m,-m} pair) and a fixed sign factor '-2(-1)^{m_o}' without deriving it from the real-basis Clebsch–Gordan transformation. The claim that 'at most one input order m_i contributes' per output m_o (i.e., a pure re-indexing) is the crux of the sparse operator, yet the real/complex change-of-basis argument is sketched rather than proven. This is the central technical novelty and needs a cleaner, checkable derivation.

No empirical test of the 'theoretical exactness' claim: there is no equivariance-error measurement (e.g., comparing rotated inputs/outputs) to verify that the sparse re-indexing reproduces the dense SO(3) tensor product, despite exactness being a key selling point.

Some accuracy framing is selective. On the SPICE 'ALL' aggregate, eSEN-Cons achieves lower energy (0.23 vs 0.31) and force (6.36 vs 7.05) MAE than E2V2-Cons, so 'achieves the lowest Energy and Force MAE across most subsets' overstates the aggregate result; the aggregate metric is also not explained.

Internal inconsistency between the main-text attention formulation (Eqs. 6–7, a QK inner-product score with radial bias/gate) and the Appendix D formulation (Eqs. 34–35, which introduce an additional non-linear edge feature Fea_ij = sigma((Q||V)⊙r)). It is unclear which is actually implemented and how the two relate.

Presentation quality is uneven: multiple typos ('EscAIP S', 'gp', duplicated citations Fu et al. 2025a/b), garbled equations in the manuscript, and the abstract's code URL is empty. These hinder verification of the kernel and model details.
